title: Number and measurement roots
lede: Latin and Greek counted differently. Learn both systems and every number word, from bicycle to gigabyte to sesquicentennial, becomes obvious.

sections.md:
## Two counting systems
English counts with **two** sets of roots: Latin and Greek. That's why a 5-sided shape is a *pentagon* (Greek) but a group of five musicians is a *quintet* (Latin).

| # | Latin | Examples | Greek | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | uni | unit, uniform, unanimous | mono | monopoly, monologue |
| 2 | bi, du | bilingual, duet, dual | di | dioxide, dilemma |
| 3 | tri | triple, trimester | tri | triangle, trilogy |
| 4 | quad, quart | quadruple, quarter | tetra | tetrahedron |
| 5 | quint | quintet, quintuple | penta | pentagon, pentathlon |
| 6 | sex | sextet | hexa | hexagon |
| 7 | sept | September | hepta | heptagon |
| 8 | oct | October, octave | octa | octagon, octopus |
| 9 | nov | November | ennea | enneagon |
| 10 | dec | December, decimal, decimate | deca | decade, decathlon |
| 100 | cent | century, percent | hecto | hectare |
| 1,000 | mill | million, millennium, mile | kilo | kilogram |

Shapes and science lean **Greek** (polygons, chemistry). Everyday life and money lean **Latin** (quarter, cents, million).

## Fractions and amounts
| Root | Meaning | Words |
|---|---|---|
| **semi, hemi, demi** | half | semifinal, semiannual; hemisphere; demigod |
| **sesqui** | one and a half | sesquicentennial (150 years) |
| **multi, poly** | many | multinational, polygon |
| **omni, pan** | all | omnivore, omnipresent; pandemic |
| **ambi, amphi** | both | ambidextrous, ambivalent; amphibian |

options: has mixed feelings, pulled both ways
sections.why: **ambi** (both) + *valent* (strong, as in value). Strongly pulled in **both** directions at once. Not the same as *indifferent* (not caring).

sections.md:
## The metric prefixes
Science and computers use one set of prefixes, set by the International System of Units (SI). Each step is a power of 10:

| Prefix | Symbol | Factor | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| tera- | T | 10¹² (trillion) | terabyte |
| giga- | G | 10⁹ (billion) | gigawatt, gigabyte |
| mega- | M | 10⁶ (million) | megahertz |
| kilo- | k | 10³ (thousand) | kilometer |
| centi- | c | 10⁻² (hundredth) | centimeter |
| milli- | m | 10⁻³ (thousandth) | millisecond |
| micro- | µ | 10⁻⁶ (millionth) | microgram |
| nano- | n | 10⁻⁹ (billionth) | nanosecond |

Notice the pattern: the **big** prefixes are Greek-derived (*mega*, great; *giga*, giant), and the **small** prefixes come from Latin numbers (*centi*, hundred; *milli*, thousand).

sections.q: How many milliseconds are in 2.5 seconds?
sections.why: **milli** = one thousandth, so 1 second = 1,000 ms. 2.5 × 1,000 = **2,500 ms**.

sections.md:
## The stories inside number words
- **September to December** mean 7th to 10th month, but they're the 9th to 12th. The early Roman calendar began in **March**, so September really was the seventh month. When January and February were later placed at the front of the year, the old names stayed.
- **Decimate** originally meant a Roman army punishment: kill **one in ten** soldiers of a mutinous unit. Today it means to destroy a large part of something.
- **Mile** comes from Latin *mille passuum*, **a thousand paces** (a Roman pace was two steps).
- **Quarantine** comes from Venetian Italian *quaranta giorni*, **forty days**: how long ships from plague areas had to wait before landing.
- **Percent** is Latin *per centum*: **by the hundred**.

sections.title: Decode a big number word
steps: One and a half hundred years.

sections.title: Decode a shape
sections.answer: A **12-sided** polygon. A dodecahedron (Greek *hedra*, seat or face) is a solid with 12 faces.

sections.md:
## The biannual trap
This is where even educated writers get burned:

| Word | Means |
|---|---|
| **biannual** | twice a year |
| **semiannual** | twice a year (clearest) |
| **biennial** | once every two years |
| **biweekly** | every two weeks **or** twice a week |

Because *biweekly* and *bimonthly* can mean either, careful writers avoid them in contracts, pay schedules and invoices. Write **every two weeks** or **twice a month** instead. That's a rule that saves real money.

sections.label: Common traps
sections.md:
- **Kilobyte confusion.** In SI, kilo = 1,000, so 1 kilobyte = 1,000 bytes. Computers count in powers of 2, so a separate set of prefixes exists for that: 1 **kibibyte** (KiB) = 1,024 bytes. That's why a "1 TB" drive shows about 931 GB in some operating systems.
- **Billion** means 10⁹ in American and modern British English, but older British usage (and many European languages) used *billion* for 10¹². In international documents, numbers beat words.

practice.q: How many years does a **sesquicentennial** celebrate?
How many sides does a **heptagon** have?
practice.why: Greek **hepta** = 7. Latin's version shows up in *September*.
**bi** (two) + **enn** (year): every two years. *Biannual* is twice a year.

practice.q: Which word uses the **Greek** root for 5?
practice.why: **penta** is Greek. *Quint* is Latin; *quince* (15) comes from it through Spanish.

practice.q: A dispatcher clocks a reply in 0.004 seconds. How many **milliseconds** is that?
Your contract says you'll be paid **"biweekly."** What's the smart move?
options: Ask them to write the exact schedule
practice.why: *Biweekly* has two dictionary meanings: every two weeks and twice a week. In anything about money, get it written exactly: "every other Friday."
practice.hint: Look at the biannual trap table again.

practice.q: **Octo**ber is the 10th month, but *octo* means 8. Why?
options: The early Roman year started in March
It was renamed after a ruler
practice.why: Count from March: March (1), April (2), May (3), June (4), July (5), August (6), September (7), **October (8)**. January and February were later put at the front, and the names never changed.

practice.q: The general's army was **decimated**. In the original Roman sense, what fraction of the soldiers died?
practice.why: **dec** = ten. Decimation killed one soldier in ten. Today the word just means *heavily destroyed*, but the root still carries the original math.
practice.hint: The root is the same as in *decimal*.
